title: Color-Emotion Associations and Color Preferences: A Case Study for Residences

findings.consequent: Color-emotion associations (DV: emotional responses to color)
findings.statement: Green color samples were associated with high frequency of positive emotional responses including excitement, relaxation, vividness, confidence, purity, auspicious, dynamism, and being serious (color samples No. 12, No. 24, No. 25).

sample.population: Turkish volunteers from various age groups

instruments_used: Polisan Natura Interior Space Color Catalogue (41 color samples)
findings.source: Table I (Frequencies of emotional responses for color samples)
findings.quote: Green samples attained the highest number of positive responses for excitement, confidence, purity, auspicious, dynamism, being serious, vivid, and striking

stimulus_description.color_catalog: Polisan Natura Interior Space Color Catalogue

findings.antecedent: Green color choice (IV: color hue) and emotional associations (IV: emotion type)
findings.consequent: Residence color selection for interiors (DV: preferred color for dwelling spaces)
findings.statement: Chi-square test showed strong dependency between green color and emotion associations in residential contexts (P = 0.043). Green was preferred for dwellings despite evoking both positive and negative emotions in the first part of the study.

sample.population: Turkish volunteers from various age groups

instruments_used: Polisan Natura Interior Space Color Catalogue
findings.source: Table III (χ² test results for color preference and residence interiors dependency)
findings.quote: χ² test results showed a strong dependency only for the color sample 'green' (P = 0.043)

stimulus_description.color_catalog: Polisan Natura Interior Space Color Catalogue

findings.antecedent: Value (lightness) and saturation (chroma) levels of yellow color samples (IV: color properties)
findings.consequent: Emotional associations with yellow (DV: emotional response type)
findings.statement: Three different yellow color samples were associated with six different emotions depending on value and saturation. Low value and high saturation yellow samples (No. 6, No. 8, No. 18) were associated with boring, fearful, tiring, anxious, annoying, depressive, and serious. Medium value and low saturation yellow samples (No. 9, No. 21, No. 32) were associated with vivid, dynamic, striking, warm, cheerful, and enjoying.

sample.population: Turkish volunteers from various age groups

instruments_used: Polisan Natura Interior Space Color Catalogue
findings.source: Results: Color-Emotion Responses section and Table I
findings.quote: Yellow color samples with low value and high saturation levels were associated with emotions such as boring, fearful, tiring, anxious, annoying, depressive, and being serious... Yellow color samples with medium value and low saturation levels were associated with feelings such as vivid, dynamic, striking, warm, cheerful, and enjoying

scope_conditions.color_samples: yellow hues: No. 6, 8, 18 (low value/high saturation); No. 9, 21, 32 (medium value/low saturation)

stimulus_description.color_catalog: Polisan Natura Interior Space Color Catalogue

findings.mechanism: Munsell color properties (value and saturation) mediate emotional associations

findings.consequent: Preference for achromatic black (DV: color preference)
findings.statement: Chi-square test indicated strong dependency between age and choice of black (P = 0.029). All participants in the fourth age group (63 years and above, n=4) preferred black.

sample.population: Turkish volunteers from various age groups

instruments_used: Polisan Natura Interior Space Color Catalogue
findings.source: Table II (χ² test results for color-age, color-gender, and color-education level dependency)
findings.quote: Test results indicated that, there was a strong dependency between age (P = 0.029)... and the choice of black. In the study, all the people in the fourth age group (63 years and above) preferred black.

stimulus_description.color_catalog: Polisan Natura Interior Space Color Catalogue

findings.consequent: Preference for achromatic black (DV: color preference)
findings.statement: Chi-square test indicated strong dependency between gender and choice of black (P = 0.031). All participants who had positive emotions towards black were female (n=30 females total).
instruments_used: Polisan Natura Interior Space Color Catalogue
findings.source: Table II (χ² test results for color-gender dependency)
findings.quote: Test results indicated that, there was a strong dependency between... gender (P = 0.031), and the choice of black. According to the study, all of the participants who had positive emotions towards black were female.

stimulus_description.color_catalog: Polisan Natura Interior Space Color Catalogue

findings.consequent: Preference for achromatic black (DV: color preference)
findings.statement: Chi-square test found no significant dependency between education level and choice of black (P = 0.836). Education level did not influence black color preference.

sample.population: Turkish volunteers from various education levels

instruments_used: Polisan Natura Interior Space Color Catalogue
findings.source: Table II (χ² test results for color-education level dependency)
findings.quote: No dependency was found between the education level and the choice of black (P = 0.836).

stimulus_description.color_catalog: Polisan Natura Interior Space Color Catalogue

findings.antecedent: Color hue (green, red, brown, blue, orange, pink, violet) and demographic factors (IV: color + age/gender/education)
findings.consequent: Color preferences across hues (DV: color preference)
findings.statement: Chi-square tests found no significant relationships between most tested colors (green, red, brown, blue, orange, pink, violet) and age, gender, or education levels. Exception: black showed significant relationships with age (P = 0.029) and gender (P = 0.031).

sample.population: Turkish volunteers from various age groups

instruments_used: Polisan Natura Interior Space Color Catalogue
findings.source: Table II showing all chi-square results
findings.quote: Except for the achromatic black, no significant relations were found among the tested colors and age, gender, and education levels as seen in Table II.

scope_conditions.colors_tested: green, red, brown, blue, orange, pink, white, violet, black

stimulus_description.color_catalog: Polisan Natura Interior Space Color Catalogue

findings.antecedent: Pink color samples, especially light pink with varied saturation (IV: pink color properties)
findings.consequent: Emotional associations and residential color preference (DV: emotion + room type selection)
findings.statement: Pink color samples (No. 16, No. 31, No. 32, No. 34) evoked feelings of enjoyment, cheerfulness, and warmness. Light pink sample No. 31 was preferred for sleeping rooms (associated with warm, romantic, enjoying emotions) and children's rooms (associated with cheerful, striking emotions).

sample.population: Turkish volunteers from various age groups

instruments_used: Polisan Natura Interior Space Color Catalogue
findings.quote: The majority of the responses indicated that the feelings of enjoyment, cheerfulness, and warmness were attained to the color samples of pink and yellow... pink sample (No. 31; the color favored for romantism, enjoyment, and warmness) were preferred for the sleeping room... the pink color sample (No. 31) was also selected for the childrens' room

stimulus_description.color_catalog: Polisan Natura Interior Space Color Catalogue

findings.antecedent: Blue color samples, specifically light blue (IV: blue color properties)
findings.consequent: Emotional associations and residential color preference (DV: emotion + room type selection)
findings.statement: Both green and blue samples (especially No. 12, No. 24, No. 25 for green; No. 40 for blue) were favored for calmness, peacefulness, relaxation, and modernism. Light blue sample No. 40 was preferred for the living room, associated with calm, peaceful, modern, relaxing emotions.

sample.population: Turkish volunteers from various age groups

instruments_used: Polisan Natura Interior Space Color Catalogue
findings.quote: Both green and blue samples were favored for calmness, peacefulness, relaxation, and modernism... the blue sample (No. 40; color favored for relaxation, calmness, peace, and modernism) was selected for the living room

stimulus_description.color_catalog: Polisan Natura Interior Space Color Catalogue

findings.antecedent: Light yellow color samples with medium-to-low saturation (IV: yellow color properties)
findings.consequent: Emotional associations and residential color preference (DV: emotion + room type selection)
findings.statement: Light yellow samples (No. 21 and No. 32) were associated with simplicity, plainness, and classicism. These samples were preferred for dining areas and entrance/stair halls, rooms associated with simple, classic, plain emotional reactions.

sample.population: Turkish volunteers from various age groups

instruments_used: Polisan Natura Interior Space Color Catalogue
findings.quote: the yellow color sample (No. 21 and No. 32; color favored for classicism, simplicity, and plainness) was offerred for the dining area... Light yellow (No. 21) Plain, simple [for entrance/stair hall]

stimulus_description.color_catalog: Polisan Natura Interior Space Color Catalogue
stimulus_description.value_saturation: medium to high value, low saturation

findings.antecedent: Near-white and light-colored samples including white, green, blue, yellow (IV: achromatic/high-value colors)
findings.consequent: Emotional associations and residential color preference (DV: emotion + room type selection)
findings.statement: Color samples close to white were associated with purity, hygiene, and cleanliness. These samples (No. 21 and near-white variants) were preferred for kitchen, bathroom, entrance, and stairhall, spaces where hygiene and purity are functionally important.

sample.population: Turkish volunteers from various age groups

instruments_used: Polisan Natura Interior Space Color Catalogue
findings.quote: color samples that were close to white were associated with purity, hygiene, and they were offerred for kitchen, bathroom, entrance, and stairhall

scope_conditions.color_samples: near-white, light green, light blue, light yellow (high value, low saturation)

stimulus_description.color_catalog: Polisan Natura Interior Space Color Catalogue

findings.mechanism: Functional room requirements (hygiene needs) align with emotional associations of near-white colors (purity, cleanliness)

findings.antecedent: Color liking preference across hue categories (IV: hue preference frequency)
findings.statement: In the study, 74.2% of participants liked orange while only 25.7% liked brown. Orange generally attained positive responses such as vivid and striking (No. 15) while brown revealed negative emotions such as dull, inauspicious, and depressive (No. 7). This difference reflects the importance of lightness and chroma over hue.

sample.population: Turkish volunteers from various age groups

instruments_used: Polisan Natura Interior Space Color Catalogue
findings.quote: In the study, 74.2% of the participants liked orange while only 25.7% liked brown. This is in accordance with the findings reported in Xin et al.; the influences of lightness and chroma were found to be much more important than that of the hue.

stimulus_description.color_catalog: Polisan Natura Interior Space Color Catalogue
stimulus_description.note: preference difference driven by value and saturation, not hue alone

findings.mechanism: Value (lightness) and saturation (chroma) properties influence hue preference more than hue category alone

limitations: Color samples used were from a single Turkish color producer (Polisan Natura), limiting generalizability to other color catalogs
All participants were Turkish with no theoretical or practical knowledge about color—findings may not generalize to color-educated populations or different cultures
Small sample size for older age group (n=4 for 63+ years); age group comparisons may be underpowered
Study was cross-sectional, not longitudinal; cannot assess temporal stability of color-emotion associations or preferences
No quantitative analysis performed for value (lightness) and saturation (chroma) at specific hue angles—categorization-based analysis only
Contradiction noted between Part 1 (green elicited depression) and Part 2 (green preferred for dwellings); unresolved by authors
No pre-registration; subject to retrospective analysis bias
Controlled laboratory lighting may not generalize to real residential lighting conditions
Participants had no color blindness screening details beyond self-report
No effect sizes reported; only p-values and frequency counts provided
